rates (daily) · dollar (daily) · stress (mixed weekly) · inflation (monthly) · positioning (weekly)

Why

▼ Pressures goldReal yields (inflation-adjusted)

Bonds that beat inflation are gold's main rival for money — the better they pay, the more a zero-yield ounce costs to hold.

EvidenceHow it works
▼ Pressures goldThe dollar against six big currencies

Gold is priced in dollars — a stronger dollar makes the same ounce pricier for buyers in every other currency, and demand tends to soften.

EvidenceHow it works
▲ Supports goldUS financial stress index

When US funding markets tighten, frightened money has historically run toward gold — the safe-haven bid at work.

EvidenceHow it works
▼ Pressures goldUS consumer inflation

Hot consumer inflation feeds gold's hedge demand — but the policy response matters more quarter-to-quarter, which is why real rates guide better at short range.

EvidenceHow it works
▼ Pressures goldTrader positioning in gold

Speculators' positioning is fuel, not a driver — at crowded extremes it marks fragile crowds; in the middle it says almost nothing.

EvidenceHow it works

What could change this: a real-yield turn, a dollar break, or a stress spike would re-weigh the balance fast.

London vault stock

London vaults hold 9,850 t of gold · data through Oct 2026

+0.29% vs the previous month

Method

Source: LBMA (London vault holdings) — monthly, one month in arrears. Holdings on the last day of the month, all physical forms within the M25 including the Bank of England's gold (the Bank holds no silver).

London clearing volumes

18.3 M oz of gold cleared in Sept 2026

18.3 M oz · $76.2 bn · 7,438 transfers

On average, more than 20 million ounces of gold is cleared daily in the London market — the net transfers settled between the four LBMA market-maker banks that own London Precious Metals Clearing (LPMCL).

Method

Source: LBMA (clearing statistics) — the net volume of gold and silver transferred between LPMCL's member banks, monthly.

The crossover lesson

Gold and real yields — the relationship that changed

The old inverse rule, its 2022 break, and the rolling correlation that shows both — no single number hides the convention.

February 2022 — the reserve freeze dated the rotation; the demand tracker above tells who stepped in.

Method

Rolling correlation: 52-week Pearson over weekly Friday closes, levels (not returns). Display window: the stored span (self-widening). Gold = XAUUSD daily closes; real yield = the 10-year TIPS yield.

How it is computed

History

Gold's big episodes

The eras that taught the market gold's lessons — the force families named under each.

1971–73Bretton Woods ends$35

The dollar left gold at $35; two devaluations followed.

family: The US dollar

1980The Volcker peak~$850

Gold touched about $850 in January 1980; disinflation then drove a two-decade bear.

family: Interest rates & borrowing costs

1999Brown's bottom~$252

The U.K. announced sales of half its gold; the price bottomed near $252.

family: Trader positioning & flows

2008The financial crisis~$1,000

Lehman's fall took gold down in the dash-for-cash; the response then lifted it.

family: Market stress & uncertainty

2011The QE-era peak~$1,920

Gold peaked near $1,920 as QE2 and the euro debt crisis peaked together.

family: Inflation & inflation expectations

2013The taper tantrum

The mere announcement of slower QE took gold down about 28% in 2013.

family: Interest rates & borrowing costs

2020COVID~$2,070

The pandemic panic and the money-printing response lifted gold to its then-record.

family: Market stress & uncertainty

2022The inflation surge

The fastest hiking cycle in four decades pressured gold all year.

family: Inflation & inflation expectations

2024–26The melt-up and correction$5,400 →

Central-bank buying and debasement worry drove the run past $5,000 — then the 2026 real-yield squeeze took a quarter of it back.

family: Interest rates & borrowing costs

the living record: 2024–26

The relationship map

How gold's forces connect

Every documented relationship, labelled with its evidence class and its own words — mechanisms, observed correlations, conditional patterns, and the causal-with-evidence records.

  • R-01Mreal-yield-10y → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Gold pays no yield, so high real returns on bonds are its classic rival — a mechanism, not a law: since 2022 the pattern weakened visibly as the marginal buyer changed.

  • R-02Mdollar-basket → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Gold is priced in dollars, so dollar strength usually weighs on the ounce — except in the two documented break patterns: stress bids and reserve-diversification bids.

  • R-03Mus10y → gold

    A yield rise is not one story but three: which piece moved — real, expected inflation, or the premium — decides what it usually means for gold.

  • R-04Cterm-premium-10y → gold

    When long yields rise because investors demand fear-and-supply compensation, history has sided with gold — except in the first, liquidity-driven phase of a stress spike.

  • R-05Mstress-stlfsi → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Frightened money historically runs to gold — but the first hours of a true panic can sell it for cash, and the haven usually arrives after policy responds.

  • R-06Cgold-silver → gold

    When gold pulls far ahead of silver, markets are paying up for pure monetary metal — a fear gauge built from the metals themselves, with silver’s industrial cycle as its known noise.

  • R-07Cgpr-daily → gold

    War and policy fear usually bid gold first and ask questions later — much of the event premium historically fades when the feared outcome doesn’t arrive.

  • R-08Minflation → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Gold's inflation hedge is earned over decades, not weeks: what matters quarter-to-quarter is how the Fed responds, which is why real rates are the better short-horizon guide.

  • R-09Mwgc-cb-demand → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Central-bank buying roughly doubled after 2022's reserve freeze — a documented demand shift that raised gold's floor; how price-insensitive it truly is remains debated, and it is no guarantee in every dip.

  • R-10Cm2-us → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    More money and bigger deficits are the decades-scale argument for gold — an association that is honest at long horizons and weak at short ones.

  • R-11Ccftc-gold-positioning → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Speculators' books are the market's fuel gauge: at the extremes they mark fragile crowds, in the middle they say almost nothing — fuel, not a driver.

  • R-12Musdjpy → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    The yen funds the world's carry trades: its calm rise eases gold's pressure, its violent surges mark the stress moments when everything, briefly, gets sold.

  • R-13Musd-reserve-share → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    When the world's official sector concentrates in dollars, gold's structural bid is quiet; when it diversifies, gold's structural story begins.

  • R-14Mborrowing-costs → dollar-basket

    Money flows toward better-paid currencies: relative rate paths drive the dollar, and the dollar is one of gold’s two great macro levers.

  • R-15Mfed-expectations → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Gold trades the expected path, not the setting: the surprise, not the move, is what usually shifts it.

  • R-16Mgold-aud → gold

    Before calling a gold move global, price it in another currency — part of every dollar-price move is just the dollar.

  • R-19Cgold-btc → gold

    The oldest and newest stores of value trade their own referendum — correlated in narrative-driven stretches, uncorrelated in most others.

  • R-20Cgold-oil-ratio → gold

    Gold, oil and platinum share the inflation tide; their ratios cancel it out and leave the relative story behind.

  • R-21Ccopper-gold → gold

    Copper bets on construction and factories; gold bets on fear — their ratio is the world's growth-versus-protection mood in one number.

  • R-22Xdollar-basket → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    In a true panic the dollar itself is the haven: gold and the dollar rise together until the panic finds its policy answer.

  • R-23Cgold-equities-ratio → gold(carries a regime/break flag)

    Stocks and gold split the risk appetite between them — sometimes opposite, sometimes together, depending on what the market is afraid of.

  • R-24Minflation → gold

    When the world's delivery chains strain, goods prices tend to feel it later — and gold feels it only after that, if the inflation sticks.

  • R-25Cmichigan-1y-expectations → gold

    Households feel inflation at the pump before markets price it in bonds — when the two expectations families disagree, the inflation story itself is contested.

  • R-26Mwgc-etf-holdings → goldblocked edge — listed, never charted

    Gold ETFs make the haven trade visible daily — inflows bid, outflows release — but this page cannot yet show that data under its licensing rules.

  • R-27Mshanghai-gold-premium → gold

    Physical gold travels to wherever it earns a premium — the flows follow the gaps with a lag, and they explain where the metal went, not why the price moved today.

Key takeaway

Gold is being pressured by high real yields, a rising dollar, and crowded long positioning; stress and monetary-hedge demand are the counterweights. The balance leans against — conditions, not a forecast.

The honest record

Every verdict on this page is derived from the same recorded readings through the same engine — nothing is double-counted, nothing invented. Dark seats state why they are dark. The balance describes conditions, never a forecast.

Publication notes — why some readings are not shown

A dark seat is dark for one of four knowable reasons: the source stopped publishing, the year-ago base month was not published (a publication gap), the data is published but the pipeline has not landed it yet, or the reading is fresh but the evaluator had no input to evaluate. Each dark seat states which one it is — the page never shows a guess.

Method: 37 voters · five lanes · equal weights · min 2 firing per lane voteData as of November 22, 2026 · Currena · gold intelligence · EN / fa — bilingual by design
